steps.prompt: What is the difference between for and since?
options: For + a length of time; since + the point it started.
For is for the past and since is for the future.
steps.answer: For + a length of time; since + the point it started.
steps.why: for five years, for six months — but since 2001, since March, since I left school.

steps.title: Present Perfect with for and since
steps.html:
FormExample
+have / has + participleI’ve worked here for five years.
+with sinceI’ve been a nurse since 2021.
–haven’t / hasn’tShe hasn’t worked here for long.
?How long …?How long have you worked here?
short answer—For six months. / Since March.
finished timePast SimpleI worked there from 2010 to 2013.

Use the Present Perfect when the situation started in the past and is still true: I’ve worked here for five years — and I still work here.

For answers “how long?”: for six months, for four years, for a long time. Since answers “from when?”: since March, since 2013, since I left school.

The question is How long have you …? — never How long do you work here? if you are still there.

If the situation is finished, go back to the Past Simple: I worked there from 2010 to 2013 — and I don’t now.

You met the Present Perfect for experiences in Lesson 17. This is its second main use.

steps.title: Four people, four desks
steps.sub: How long, and what the day actually looks like.
steps.html:
Reading

We asked four people the same question: how long have you done this, and what does a day actually look like?

Zhanna, accountant, 11 years. “I’ve worked in the same office since 2013 and I still like it. People think an accountant counts money all day. I don’t. I answer enquiries, I check things other people have signed, and I explain the same rule to somebody new about twice a week. The numbers take an hour. The rest is people.”

Ruslan, nurse, 4 years. “I’ve been a nurse for four years and I have never had a typical day. I know when my shift starts. I don’t know anything else. Most of the job is not medical: it is explaining, in normal words, what somebody has just been told by a doctor in words they did not understand.”

Kamila, software developer, 6 months. “I’ve only been here since March, so I am still the newest person in the room. I write code for about three hours a day. The other five hours are meetings, messages and reading what other people wrote before I arrived. Nobody tells you that at university.”

Dias, court administrator, 19 years. “I’ve run the day-to-day business of this court since 2006. We set the dates, we answer the phone, we deal with the paperwork. It is not the most exciting job in the world. But when something goes wrong here, it goes wrong for a real family. So I have never been bored.”

Eleven years, four years, six months, nineteen years. Four very different answers to “what do you do all day?” — and not one of them matched the job title.

steps.answer: The job title does not describe what the person actually does.
